papers.title: Covariance Nonstationarity is Evident in Spatial Transcriptomics and Provides a New Categorization of Spatially Varying Genes
papers.summary: This paper argues that gene expression covariance in spatial transcriptomics data is not uniform across tissue space, meaning the relationships between genes change from region to region rather than staying constant. Based on this observation, the authors propose a new way to classify spatially varying genes according to how their covariance structure shifts locally. This offers an alternative to standard approaches that assume stationary spatial statistics when identifying spatially variable genes.
papers.why: Since the PhD project relies on spatial transcriptomics to map gene expression patterns around neurons, interneurons, and perineuronal nets, recognizing covariance nonstationarity could improve how spatially varying genes are identified and interpreted in these datasets.
papers.figure: A figure showing spatial maps of local covariance structure across tissue regions alongside the resulting gene categorization scheme.

papers.title: Wiring autophagy: Neural circuits regulate lysosomal homeostasis in muscle.
papers.summary: This paper explores how neural circuits influence lysosomal homeostasis in muscle tissue, suggesting that autophagy regulation extends beyond individual cells to be coordinated by nervous system signaling. It implies that specific neural inputs can 'wire' or program the degradative capacity of peripheral tissues like muscle. This connects broader organismal physiology and behavior to the cell-autonomous machinery of autophagy and lysosomal function.
papers.why: While focused on muscle rather than brain, this study offers a valuable conceptual parallel for understanding how neural circuit activity regulates autophagy/lysosomal pathways, which may inform hypotheses about neuronal mitophagy regulation in interneurons.

papers.title: Emerging roles of mitophagy in liver fibrosis: Implications for therapy.
papers.summary: This paper reviews mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared, and its role in liver fibrosis development. It discusses how dysregulated mitophagy in liver cells contributes to fibrotic scarring and disease progression. The review also highlights potential therapeutic strategies that target mitophagy pathways to treat liver fibrosis.
papers.why: This paper is only tangentially relevant since it focuses on hepatic mitophagy rather than neuronal mitophagy and autophagy mechanisms central to the profile's brain-focused research.

papers.title: Melatonin attenuates burn-wound progression by inhibiting inflammation via mitophagy-related pathway.
papers.summary: This study looks at melatonin's effect on preventing burn wounds from getting worse. The researchers found that melatonin reduces inflammation at the wound site. They suggest this happens through a pathway related to mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria.
papers.why: Although this paper is about skin burns rather than the brain, it studies mitophagy-related pathways as a mechanism for reducing inflammation, which could offer tangential mechanistic insight relevant to mitophagy processes in neurons.

papers.title: Inhibition of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy enhances the susceptibility of breast cancer to cuproptosis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how blocking PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy—the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria—affects breast cancer cells' vulnerability to cuproptosis, a form of copper-induced cell death. The researchers likely show that when mitophagy is inhibited, damaged mitochondria accumulate, making cancer cells more sensitive to dying via cuproptosis. This suggests a potential therapeutic strategy combining mitophagy inhibitors with copper-based treatments for breast cancer.
papers.why: Although focused on cancer rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy regulation that is directly relevant to understanding mitophagy pathways studied in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: FOXO1 Promotes Mitophagy in Granulosa Cells by Targeting the METTL3/SMAD4 axis.
papers.summary: This study finds that FOXO1, a transcription factor, promotes mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) in ovarian granulosa cells. It does so by regulating an axis involving METTL3 (an RNA methyltransferase) and SMAD4 (a signaling protein). The work likely has implications for understanding ovarian reserve and fertility through mitochondrial quality control.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on granulosa cells rather than neurons, the core mitophagy regulatory mechanism involving FOXO1-mediated control of mitochondrial quality control pathways could offer conceptual parallels or contrast points for understanding mitophagy regulation in neurons.

papers.title: Autophagy in Osx1-Cre-targeted cells is essential for development, growth, and maintenance of bone.
papers.summary: This paper studies mice where autophagy genes are deleted specifically in Osx1-Cre-targeted cells, which are osteoblast precursors involved in bone formation. The researchers found that loss of autophagy in these cells impairs bone development, growth, and long-term maintenance. This suggests autophagy is a critical cellular process for skeletal health.
papers.why: This paper is about bone biology and osteoblast autophagy, which is largely outside the core focus on neuronal mitophagy, interneurons, and perineuronal nets in the brain.
